title: Nearest charging stations
statement:
Charging stations are given as `[x, y]` points on a map, and your car is at the origin `[0, 0]`. Return the `k` stations closest to the car by straight-line distance, in any order.

The answer is guaranteed to be unique: there is never a tie at the kth place.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is distance straight-line (Euclidean)?
clarifyingQuestions.why: Defines the comparison; you can compare squared distances and skip the square root.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can there be ties at the kth place?
Does the output order matter?
clarifyingQuestions.why: You do not need to sort the final k.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many stations, and how big is k?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 10,000 stations; k can be anywhere from 1 to the number of stations.
clarifyingQuestions.why: Decides between sorting, a heap, or quickselect.

edgeCases.input: k equals the number of stations

approaches.name: Sort by distance
approaches.idea: Sort all stations by squared distance and take the first k.

approaches.name: Max-heap of size k
approaches.idea: Keep the k closest seen so far in a max-heap keyed by distance; when it grows past k, drop the farthest.
approaches.tradeoffs: Better when k is small; works on a stream.

approaches.name: Quickselect
approaches.idea: Partition around a pivot distance until the first k positions hold the k closest.
approaches.tradeoffs: Fastest on average, more complex and unstable worst case.

optimal.name: Size-k max-heap
optimal.explanation: For each station compute d = x^2 + y^2 and push (-d, station) onto a min-heap, which acts as a max-heap on d. If the heap holds more than k items, pop, removing the farthest. The heap ends with the k closest.

hintLadder: Do you need the actual distance, or just a way to compare distances?
Do you need everything sorted, or only the k best?
How can you keep the best k as you go and know which one to drop?
Keep a max-heap of size k on squared distance and drop the farthest whenever it overflows.

expectedMentions.what: Asks about ties, output order or the size of k
Notes comparing squared distances avoids square roots
Mentions sorting all stations, O(n log n)
Proposes a size-k heap and states O(n log k)
Explains why the heap evicts the farthest (max-heap)

followUps: Stations arrive as a stream; keep the k nearest at all times.
The car moves; answer many queries quickly.

walkthrough.say: Straight-line distance from the origin, no ties at the kth spot, and any order in the output?
I only need to compare distances, so I can use x squared plus y squared and skip the square root. The easy answer is to sort by that and take k, n log n.

If k is small, a max-heap of size k is better: I keep the k closest so far, and when a closer one arrives I evict the farthest. That’s n log k. Python’s heapq is a min-heap, so I’ll push negative distances.
Push each station; trim to k.

Example: distances are 25, 2, 8 and 25. With k of 2, after the first two the heap has 25 and 2. Adding 8 makes three, pop the largest, 25. Adding 5, 0 at 25 makes three, pop 25 again. Left with 1, -1 and -2, 2.
If k equals the number of stations, nothing is ever popped, so I return them all.
O(n log k) time, O(k) space. Quickselect would get average linear time if needed.
